title: Nobel week, AI copies and a state-run dating app

stories.headline: South African judge Navi Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize
stories.headlineZh: 南非法官纳维·皮莱获诺贝尔和平奖
stories.summaryZh: 85 岁的前联合国人权事务高级专员因推动国际法获奖，评委会借此强调“以法止战”。
stories.b2:
Navi Pillay, a South African judge who spent her career making sure the powerful could be held to account, has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee said the 85-year-old had greatly broadened the scope and impact of international law. Announcing the prize in Oslo, committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes called her work a source of hope for everyone trying to build a more peaceful world. The committee admitted it had not yet been able to reach her with the news.

Pillay began her career under apartheid, working as a lawyer for opponents of the regime. In 1995 she became the first non-white woman to sit on South Africa's High Court. She went on to serve as a judge, and later as president, of the international tribunal set up to prosecute those responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. She then joined the International Criminal Court and, from 2008 to 2014, led the United Nations' human rights office.

In its statement, the committee warned that conflicts are multiplying while judges and international courts face mounting political attacks. Its message was that lasting peace rests on the rule of law: a legal system in which war criminals face justice and victims are heard.

The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, will be presented on 10 December.
stories.c1:
At a moment when international justice is under unusual strain, the Norwegian Nobel Committee has chosen to honour one of its most steadfast defenders. The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize goes to Navi Pillay, the 85-year-old South African judge who, in the committee's words, has substantially broadened the scope and impact of international law.

Pillay's career traces the arc of modern international justice. She began as a lawyer representing opponents of South Africa's apartheid government and, in 1995, became the first non-white woman appointed to the country's High Court. From there she moved onto the global stage, serving as a judge and later president of the UN tribunal established to try those responsible for the 1994 Rwandan genocide, then as a judge at the International Criminal Court, before heading the UN human rights office from 2008 to 2014. Throughout, her work has turned on a single question: whether those who commit atrocities can be held to account.

The choice carries an unmistakable message. In announcing the award, the committee pointed to a rising number of wars and to mounting political attacks on judges and international courts, arguing that the peaceful resolution of conflict ultimately rests on the rule of law. In its view, accountability for war crimes and justice for victims are not optional extras but preconditions for lasting peace.

Tellingly, the committee had been unable to contact Pillay before revealing her name to the world. The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, will be presented in Oslo on 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death.

vocab.en: experiencing pressure that makes something difficult to maintain
vocab.example: Hospitals are under strain during the winter flu season.

vocab.en: to make something cover more areas or situations
vocab.example: The new law broadens the scope of consumer protection.

vocab.en: made to explain and take responsibility for your actions
vocab.example: Companies that pollute rivers should be held to account.

vocab.en: so clear that it cannot be confused with anything else
vocab.example: There was an unmistakable sense of relief in the room.

vocab.en: gradually increasing
vocab.example: The government faces mounting pressure to act on housing.

vocab.en: to depend on something as a basis
vocab.example: The success of the plan rests on public support.

vocab.en: the principle that everyone, including the government, must obey the law
vocab.example: Foreign investors want countries with a strong rule of law.

vocab.en: the fact of being responsible for what you do and able to explain it
vocab.example: Voters are demanding greater accountability from politicians.

vocab.en: something that must exist before something else can happen
vocab.example: Trust is a precondition for any successful negotiation.

questions.q: Pillay led the UN human rights office before she became a judge at the International Criminal Court.
questions.explain: 原文顺序是先在国际刑事法院当法官，之后（2008–2014）才领导联合国人权办公室：then as a judge at the International Criminal Court, before heading the UN human rights office。判断题常在时间先后上设陷阱。

questions.q: The committee told Pillay about the award before announcing it publicly.
questions.explain: 原文：the committee had been unable to contact Pillay before revealing her name——宣布前没能联系上她。

questions.q: Pillay plans to donate the prize money to human rights organisations.
questions.explain: 文中完全没有提到奖金用途，所以是 Not Given。

questions.q: What is the main message behind the committee's choice?
options: International courts should replace national governments
Peace ultimately depends on the rule of law and accountability
The UN should spend more money on human rights
War crimes are becoming less common
questions.explain: 评委会认为和平最终取决于法治（rests on the rule of law），问责是持久和平的前提。

stories.discuss: Why might some countries refuse to cooperate with international courts? Do you think this will change in the future?

stories.headline: The physicist who turned Antarctic ice into a telescope wins a Nobel
stories.headlineZh: 把南极冰层变成望远镜的物理学家获诺贝尔奖
stories.summaryZh: 哈尔森 1988 年提出用南极冰探测中微子，IceCube 观测站让他独得 2026 年诺贝尔物理学奖。
stories.b2:
In 1988, Francis Halzen proposed an idea that sounded like a long shot: use the ice beneath the South Pole as a giant particle detector. Almost four decades later, that idea has earned him the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics.

The Belgian-born physicist, now 82 and based at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, was honoured for his decisive role in building the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space.

Neutrinos are nicknamed “ghost particles” because they are so elusive: they barely interact with matter. Tens of billions pass through your fingertip every second without leaving a trace. On the rare occasions when one does strike an atom, it gives off a faint flash of blue light. IceCube catches those flashes with 5,160 sensors buried in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice. Because neutrinos travel in straight lines, scientists can pinpoint the violent cosmic events that produced them.

The detector was completed in 2011, and two years later it produced the first evidence of neutrinos from far beyond our solar system. The Nobel Committee praised Halzen's tenacity and vision. Unusually for physics, he won the prize alone, and he used the moment to thank the colleagues who joined the project in its early days. His team is now planning a successor about eight times larger.
stories.c1:
When Francis Halzen suggested in 1988 that the ice sheet beneath the South Pole could double as a particle detector, the proposal sounded far-fetched. Nearly four decades on, it has earned the Belgian-born physicist the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, which he receives alone, an increasingly rare distinction in a field dominated by large collaborations.

Halzen, 82, who has spent most of his career at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, was recognised for his decisive contribution to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos originating far beyond our solar system. Neutrinos are notoriously elusive: they carry no electric charge, have almost no mass and pass through ordinary matter virtually unimpeded. Tens of billions of them stream through every square centimetre of your skin each second without leaving any trace.

The breakthrough lay in exploiting that elusiveness rather than fighting it. On the rare occasions when a neutrino does collide with an atom in the ice, it produces a faint flash of blue light. IceCube's 5,160 sensors, embedded in a cubic kilometre of exceptionally clear Antarctic ice, record these flashes, and because neutrinos travel in straight lines, researchers can work backwards to pinpoint the violent cosmic events that produced them.

Completed in 2011, the observatory delivered its first evidence of astrophysical neutrinos two years later, opening what the Nobel Committee described as a new kind of astronomy. Halzen has credited the colleagues who backed the idea when it looked like a long shot, and his team is already planning a successor roughly eight times larger.

vocab.en: very unlikely to be true or to succeed
vocab.example: The plot of the film was entertaining but completely far-fetched.

vocab.en: to have a second use or job
vocab.example: The sofa doubles as a bed for guests.

vocab.en: something that has only a small chance of succeeding
vocab.example: It's a long shot, but it's worth applying.

vocab.en: a special honour or achievement
vocab.example: She has the distinction of being the youngest ever winner.

vocab.en: in a way that is well known, usually for something bad
vocab.example: Melbourne's weather is notoriously unpredictable.

vocab.zh: 难以捉摸的；难以找到的
vocab.en: difficult to find, catch or achieve
vocab.example: A lasting solution remains elusive.

vocab.en: not slowed or stopped by anything
vocab.example: Traffic flowed unimpeded after the road reopened.

vocab.en: to use something in a way that helps you
vocab.example: The company exploited its early lead in the market.

vocab.en: to find or describe something exactly
vocab.example: Engineers finally pinpointed the cause of the fault.

questions.q: Halzen shared the 2026 physics prize with other members of the IceCube team.
questions.explain: 原文：which he receives alone——他是独自获奖。

questions.q: Neutrinos can pass through ordinary matter with almost no resistance.
questions.explain: pass through ordinary matter virtually unimpeded = 几乎毫无阻碍地穿过普通物质，与题干同义替换。

questions.q: IceCube was the first scientific experiment ever built at the South Pole.
questions.explain: 文章没有比较 IceCube 和南极其他实验的先后，属于 Not Given。

questions.q: Why can researchers work out where a detected neutrino came from?
options: Neutrinos record the temperature of their source
Each neutrino produces a different colour of light
questions.explain: because neutrinos travel in straight lines, researchers can work backwards——直线传播所以能反推来源。

stories.discuss: Should governments spend large amounts of public money on scientific research that has no obvious practical use? Why or why not?

stories.headline: Artists say Etsy is filling up with AI copies of their work
stories.headlineZh: 手工平台 Etsy 被 AI 仿品淹没，创作者叫苦
stories.summaryZh: 霍巴特的钩针设计师发现自己的爆款图案被 AI 仿制出售；法律专家称版权法难以保护“风格”。
stories.b2:
For years, Etsy has marketed itself as a home for handmade goods. Now buyers and sellers say the platform is being flooded with AI-generated products, some of which copy real artists' work.

Lucy Cooper, a 21-year-old crochet designer from Hobart, learned this the hard way. Her spiral beanie, inspired by 1990s surfwear, went viral on social media, so she began selling the pattern on Etsy. Months later, she stumbled upon another shop offering an AI-generated version of it, complete with AI images. Customers who bought the copy told her the instructions simply didn't produce the hat. When the ABC checked, that seller had made around 720 sales.

Etsy says its rules are centred on human creativity. Sellers may use AI as a tool, the company says, but not to deceive buyers or copy others, and it concedes that enforcing this across such a huge marketplace is difficult.

The law offers limited help. Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson points out that copyright protects a specific work, not a style, so an AI imitation that isn't identical may not break the law. She argues that artists urgently need clearer guidance on their rights.
stories.c1:
Etsy built its brand on the promise of the handmade; its stated mission is to “keep commerce human”. Yet a growing chorus of buyers and sellers now complains that the marketplace is being swamped by AI-generated products, some of them thinly disguised copies of real artists' designs.

The experience of Lucy Cooper, a 21-year-old crochet designer from Hobart, is a case in point. After a spiral beanie she created, inspired by 1990s surfwear, went viral, she began selling the pattern on Etsy. A few months later she stumbled upon another shop offering what appeared to be an AI-generated imitation, illustrated with AI images. Several customers who had bought it reported that the instructions simply did not produce the hat. When the ABC checked, the seller had racked up roughly 720 sales.

Etsy insists that its standards are centred on human creativity: sellers may use AI as a tool, but not to mislead customers or replicate other people's work. The company concedes, however, that policing a platform of its size is complex and that there is more work to do.

The legal picture is murkier still. Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson notes that public debate has focused on what AI systems are trained on rather than on what they produce. Because copyright protects a particular work rather than a style, an AI-generated variation that stops short of an exact copy may not breach the law. Artists, she argues, urgently need clarity about their rights and about how to enforce them.

vocab.zh: 越来越多（人发出同样声音）
vocab.en: an increasing number of people saying the same thing
vocab.example: A growing chorus of experts is calling for stricter rules.

vocab.en: overwhelmed by too much of something
vocab.example: The help desk was swamped with calls after the outage.

vocab.zh: 稍加掩饰的；换汤不换药的
vocab.en: only slightly hidden, so the truth is easy to see
vocab.example: His question was a thinly disguised criticism.

vocab.en: a clear example of what has just been said
vocab.example: Public transport can be unreliable; last night's delays are a case in point.

vocab.en: to find something by chance
vocab.example: I stumbled upon a great café while exploring the laneways.

vocab.en: to gradually collect a large number or amount of something
vocab.example: The video racked up a million views in two days.

vocab.en: to admit that something is true, often unwillingly
vocab.example: The minister conceded that mistakes had been made.

vocab.en: unclear and complicated
vocab.example: The rules around data ownership remain murky.

vocab.zh: 差一点就……；没有走到……的地步
vocab.en: to almost do something but not actually do it
vocab.example: The report stopped short of blaming the company directly.

questions.q: Etsy does not allow sellers to use AI tools in any way.
questions.explain: 原文：sellers may use AI as a tool——可以把 AI 当工具，只是不能误导买家或抄袭。

questions.q: Buyers of the copied pattern were unable to make the hat by following it.
questions.explain: the instructions simply did not produce the hat——照着做织不出那顶帽子。

questions.q: Etsy has removed the shop that copied Cooper's design.
questions.explain: 文章没有说 Etsy 是否下架了那家店，属于 Not Given。

questions.q: According to Professor Paterson, why might an AI-generated variation be legal?
options: AI companies have paid for the right to copy designs
Copyright protects particular works rather than styles
Etsy owns all designs sold on its platform
Crochet patterns are not considered creative works
questions.explain: copyright protects a particular work rather than a style——版权保护具体作品而非风格。

stories.discuss: Do you think AI-generated art and design will reduce the value of human creativity? Why or why not?

stories.headline: Singapore launches a dating app just for public servants
stories.headlineZh: 新加坡推出公务员专属婚恋 App
stories.summaryZh: 生育率跌至 0.87 的新加坡用算法为 21–35 岁公务员“一次只配一人”，专家怀疑能否扭转趋势。
stories.b2:
Singapore has entered the dating business. This month the government rolled out FirstDate, a matchmaking app open only to public servants aged 21 to 35 who verify their identity through Singpass, the national digital ID system.

Instead of an endless feed of profiles, FirstDate offers one match at a time. Users answer questions about their interests, habits and values, and an algorithm based on the Gale-Shapley “stable marriage” model, devised by two American mathematicians in 1962, pairs them up. Matches have three days to decide whether to connect, and couples who meet can claim government vouchers for organised “date quests”.

The reason is demographic. Singapore's fertility rate dropped to a record low of 0.87 children per woman in 2025, and the number of marriages fell by 6.2 per cent. The government has already promised S$70,000 in support for every child from birth to age 17.

Researchers doubt that an algorithm can turn the tide. One expert notes that high housing costs, the rising cost of living and work pressure remain untouched. Another sees the app as part of a wider pattern in Asia, where cities such as Tokyo and Seoul run their own matchmaking schemes.
stories.c1:
Singapore's government has added matchmaking to its long list of policy tools. This month it rolled out FirstDate, a dating app open exclusively to public servants aged 21 to 35, who must verify their identity through Singpass, the national digital ID system.

The app deliberately rejects the endless-scroll model of commercial dating platforms. Users answer questions about their interests, habits and values, and an algorithm based on the Gale-Shapley “stable marriage” model, devised by two American mathematicians in 1962, proposes a single match at a time. Each pair has three days to decide whether to connect, and couples who meet up can redeem government vouchers for organised “date quests”.

The rationale is demographic. Singapore's total fertility rate sank to a record low of 0.87 children per woman in 2025, while the number of marriages fell by 6.2 per cent. Officials have already pledged S$70,000 in support for every child from birth to age 17, yet the downward trend has proved stubborn.

Researchers are sceptical that better matchmaking can turn the tide. One academic argues that the underlying pressures, from high housing costs to the rising cost of living and demanding work cultures, are left untouched by an algorithm. Another frames FirstDate as part of a broader pattern across East Asia, where cities such as Tokyo and Seoul now run state-backed matchmaking schemes, effectively casting the government in the role of an anxious parent.

vocab.en: to introduce a new product or service
vocab.example: The bank will roll out the new app next month.

vocab.en: only for a particular person or group
vocab.example: The lounge is exclusively for members.

vocab.en: the reasons behind a decision or belief
vocab.example: The rationale for the policy was never clearly explained.

vocab.en: the lowest level ever recorded
vocab.example: Unemployment fell to a record low last year.

vocab.en: to make a serious promise
vocab.example: Both parties have pledged to cut emissions.

vocab.en: difficult to change or remove
vocab.example: Inflation has proved more stubborn than expected.

vocab.en: to change a situation to the opposite direction
vocab.example: A late goal turned the tide in their favour.

vocab.en: real and basic, but not always obvious
vocab.example: We need to address the underlying causes of the problem.

vocab.en: supported or funded by the government
vocab.example: The state-backed loan scheme helps first-home buyers.

questions.q: Any Singaporean citizen aged 21 to 35 can sign up for FirstDate.
questions.explain: open exclusively to public servants——仅限公务员，不是所有公民。

questions.q: Couples who meet through the app can receive government vouchers.
questions.explain: couples who meet up can redeem government vouchers——见面的情侣可兑换政府代金券。

questions.q: More than 10,000 public servants joined the app in its first week.
questions.explain: 文中没有给出注册人数，属于 Not Given。

questions.q: Why are experts doubtful that the app will raise the birth rate?
options: Deeper pressures such as housing costs and work culture remain
Public servants are too busy to date
Similar schemes in Tokyo and Seoul failed completely
questions.explain: 专家认为高房价、生活成本和工作压力等根本问题（underlying pressures）没有改变。

stories.discuss: Why do you think many young people today are choosing to marry later, or not at all?

dialogue.title: Chatting about the news
dialogue.setting: Two classmates, Mia and Leo, meet outside the seminar room.
dialogue.settingZh: 两位同学 Mia 和 Leo 在研讨课教室门口碰面，聊起这周的新闻。

lines.name: Mia
lines.en: Did you catch the Nobel announcements this week? It's been a big one.
lines.zh: 你看这周的诺贝尔奖公布了吗？挺热闹的。

lines.name: Leo
lines.en: Only bits and pieces. The Peace Prize went to a judge, didn't it?
lines.zh: 只看了一点点。和平奖是给了一位法官吧？

lines.name: Mia
lines.en: Yeah, Navi Pillay. Apparently the committee couldn't even get hold of her before announcing it.
lines.zh: 对，纳维·皮莱。听说委员会宣布之前都没联系上她。

lines.name: Leo
lines.en: That's wild. Imagine finding out from the news like everyone else!
lines.zh: 太离谱了。想象一下和大家一样从新闻里得知自己获奖！

lines.name: Mia
lines.en: Right? And the physics prize went to the guy behind that neutrino detector buried in Antarctic ice.
lines.zh: 是吧？物理学奖给了那个把中微子探测器埋在南极冰里的人。

lines.name: Leo
lines.en: Oh, I read about that. It sounded completely far-fetched at first, but it actually worked.
lines.zh: 哦，我看到了。一开始听着完全不靠谱，结果真成了。

lines.name: Mia
lines.en: Exactly. Thirty-odd years of sticking with one idea. You've got to admire that kind of persistence.
lines.zh: 就是。坚持一个想法三十多年，这种毅力真让人佩服。

lines.name: Leo
lines.en: Totally. On a less inspiring note, did you see the story about AI copies flooding Etsy?
lines.zh: 确实。说个不那么励志的，你看到 Etsy 被 AI 仿品淹没的新闻了吗？

lines.name: Mia
lines.en: I did. It's a bit of a grey area legally, which is the frustrating part.
lines.zh: 看了。法律上算是灰色地带，这才是最让人头疼的。

lines.name: Leo
lines.en: Yeah, copyright doesn't really cover style, from what I understand.
lines.zh: 嗯，据我了解，版权其实不保护风格。

lines.name: Mia
lines.en: Which basically means artists are left to fend for themselves.
lines.zh: 那基本上就是让创作者自生自灭了。

lines.name: Leo
lines.en: Pretty much. Anyway, we'd better head in. The seminar's about to kick off.
lines.zh: 差不多吧。好了，我们进去吧，研讨课要开始了。

phrases.zh: catch = 碰巧看到/听到，比 see 更地道
只知道零零碎碎的一点
三十多年（-odd 表示“多一点”）

phrases.en: It's a bit of a grey area legally.
they're left to fend for themselves
phrases.zh: 只能自己想办法；自生自灭
